This document derives that, simulates it, and checks it against the published models." categories: [pharmacometrics, identifiability, immunology, working document] date: last-modified toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-location: left toc-expand: true number-sections: false html-math-method: mathjax execute: freeze: auto warning: false message: false --- ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} **The simulations here run on every render and the published numbers do not.** Everything computed on this page comes from the code chunks in it, with parameter values chosen to resemble published models and stated where they are chosen. The published estimates in Section 8 were transcribed from the papers by a fetch tool and carry ⚠️ in [references.qmd](references.qmd); the theory sources are from abstracts and carry ❌. The [project index](index.qmd) lists the other documents in this folder. This project grew out of Section 6.2 of the [ITP-PK-Platelet specification](../imm-itp-pk-platelet/specification.qmd). ::: ## In brief **The question.** A monoclonal antibody depletes circulating B cells. The standard model is an indirect response with the drug raising the B-cell loss rate through $E_{\max} C / (EC_{50} + C)$. Published fits of this model report $E_{\max}$ near 150, and either report $EC_{50}$ with a wide interval, or fix it, or give up on it and fit a slope instead. Is $EC_{50}$ estimable at all, and if so from what? **The answer.** ⚠️ **$EC_{50}$ is estimable only through $E_{\max}$, and $E_{\max}$ is estimable only from the first days of depletion or from a cohort held in a concentration band two orders of magnitude below $EC_{50}$. With a first post-dose B-cell sample at a week and doses that deplete completely, the two parameters are perfectly correlated and only their ratio is identified.** Three quantities in the data carry three pieces of information: the recovery tail carries $k_{\rm out}$; the speed of the initial fall carries $k_{\rm out} E_{\max}$; the timing of the recovery's start carries $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. Lose the first days, and the second piece is gone, and $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ collapse onto one ridge. Section 2 derives each of these from the model equation, Section 5 shows them in the sensitivities, and Section 6 puts numbers on them by design. **Why a large $E_{\max}$ makes it worse.** The nadir is $B_0/(1 + E)$. With $E_{\max} = 150$, the count at $C = EC_{50}$ is already 1.3% of baseline, below any flow-cytometry limit. Half-maximal *depletion* happens at $C \approx EC_{50}/150$. The concentration band over which the cell count can say anything about $EC_{50}$ separately from $E_{\max}$ is therefore far below every therapeutic dose, and usually below the PK assay. Section 4. **What to do instead.** Parameterize the drug effect as the slope $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, which is what Schoemaker et al. proposed in 1998 for exactly this situation and what the inebilizumab model did in 2022, and test the $E_{\max}$ form only when a cohort has a quantifiable nadir. Section 9. Everything downstream that depends on the duration of depletion depends on the slope and $k_{\rm out}$, and loses nothing. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Recovery tail
days 150 to 300"] --> K["k_out"] B["Speed of the fall
days 0 to 3"] --> KE["k_out × Emax"] C["When recovery starts
days 80 to 140"] --> R["Emax / EC50"] K --> KE KE --> E["Emax"] E --> R R --> EC["EC50"] ``` **Out of scope, stated once.** - ❌ **Target-mediated drug disposition.** The PK here is linear. Where a published model ties the effect to receptor occupancy with a binding constant fixed from in vitro data, that is a different route to the same place and Section 8 notes it. - ❌ **Tissue B cells.** Only the circulating count is modelled, because only it is measured. - ❌ **Any recommendation about a named drug's dose.** The compounds in Section 8 are sources of parameter values and of what happened when the model was fit. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 1. The model An indirect response model of the fourth Jusko type: the drug stimulates the loss of the response variable. With $B$ the circulating B-cell count, $$ \frac{dB}{dt} = k_{\rm in} - k_{\rm out}\,\big(1 + E(C)\big)\,B, \qquad E(C) = \frac{E_{\max}\, C}{EC_{50} + C}, \qquad B(0) = B_0 = \frac{k_{\rm in}}{k_{\rm out}} $$ and one-compartment PK after an intravenous bolus, $C(t) = (D/V) e^{-k_e t}$. | Symbol | What it is | Value used here | Why that value | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | $B_0$ | Baseline B-cell count | 200 cells/µL | Typical adult; ofatumumab model 194, inebilizumab 135 | | $k_{\rm out}$ | B-cell loss rate; sets the repopulation speed | 0.02 per day | Half-life 35 d; ofatumumab 0.0124/d, paediatric rituximab CD19 half-life 173 d | | $E_{\max}$ | Maximum fold-increase in loss rate | 150 | Ofatumumab 159, paediatric rituximab 155 | | $EC_{50}$ | Concentration for half of $E_{\max}$ | 1 mg/L | Arbitrary scale; only $C/EC_{50}$ enters | | $V$, $CL$ | Volume, clearance | 3 L, 0.2 L/day | Half-life 10.4 d, an IgG1 antibody | | LOQ | Flow-cytometry limit for B cells | 5 or 10 cells/µL | 2.5% or 5% of baseline | | $\sigma$ | Proportional residual error | 30% | Inebilizumab model 61%, ofatumumab lower; 30% is generous to the design | : Parameters of the simulated system {tbl-colwidths="[12,34,20,34]"} The published values are in [references.qmd](references.qmd), entries 5 to 8, transcribed and not verified. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2); a single-hue ramp for dose. pal3 <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a") ramp5 <- c("#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c") Emax <- 150; EC50 <- 1; kout <- 0.02; B0 <- 200; V <- 3; CL <- 0.2 # The model: one-compartment PK after an IV bolus into A, and B cells made at # kout * B0 and lost at kout * (1 + E(C)). slope = 1 swaps the Emax drug effect # for the log-linear slope form used in Section 9. bcell <- rxode2({ C <- A / V if (slope == 1) { E <- S * log(1 + C / Cref) } else { E <- Emax * C / (EC50 + C) } d/dt(A) <- -CL / V * A B(0) <- B0 d/dt(B) <- kout * B0 - kout * (1 + E) * B }) # B-cell count at the requested times after a single dose. Tight tolerances, # because Sections 5 and 6 take finite differences of the output. sim_B <- function(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0 = 200, times, form = "emax", S = 0, Cref = 1) { ev <- et(amt = dose, cmt = "A") %>% et(times) p <- c(Emax = Emax, EC50 = EC50, kout = kout, B0 = B0, V = V, CL = CL, slope = as.numeric(form == "slope"), S = S, Cref = Cref) out <- rxSolve(bcell, p, ev, atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10, returnType = "data.frame") out$B[match(times, out$time)] } ``` ::: ## 2. Which part of the curve carries which parameter **After a single depleting dose, the B-cell curve has five parts, and each is set by one parameter or one combination of parameters: the baseline by $B_0$, the fall by $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$, the floor by $E_{\max}$, the time the count climbs back by $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, and the tail by $k_{\rm out}$. No part is set by $EC_{50}$ alone.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f_loq <- 0.05; ke <- CL / V; S0 <- Emax / EC50 # A: the model, drawn pA <- ggplot() + annotate("rect", xmin = c(0.7, 2.7), xmax = c(1.3, 3.3), ymin = 1.7, ymax = 2.3, fill = "grey88", colour = "grey40") + annotate("text", x = c(1, 3), y = 2, label = c("C", "B"), size = 6) + annotate("segment", x = c(1, 1, 3, 3), xend = c(1, 1, 3, 3), y = c(3, 1.7, 3, 1.7), yend = c(2.3, 1, 2.3, 1), arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))) + annotate("text", x = c(1.08, 0.92, 3.08, 3.08), y = c(2.65, 1.35, 2.65, 1.35), hjust = c(0, 1, 0, 0), size = 3.2, parse = TRUE, label = c("Dose", "k[e] == CL/V", "k[out]*B[0]", "k[out]*(1 + E(C))")) + annotate("curve", x = 1.3, y = 1.85, xend = 2.95, yend = 1.3, linetype = 2, curvature = 0.25, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), colour = "grey40") + annotate("text", x = 1.9, y = 0.85, parse = TRUE, size = 3.2, label = "E(C) == frac(E[max]*C, EC[50] + C)") + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 4.5), ylim = c(0.5, 3.1)) + theme_void() + labs(title = "A. Five parts of the curve") # C: climb-back time across doses, simulated and from the formula t_climb <- function(dose, Emax, EC50) { tt <- seq(0, 600, by = 0.5); B <- sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt) i <- which.min(B); if (B[i] >= f_loq * B0) return(NA) tt[i - 1 + which(B[i:length(B)] >= f_loq * B0)[1]] } sets <- data.frame(Emax = c(50, 150, 450, 150), EC50 = c(1/3, 1, 3, 10)) sets$set <- sprintf("Emax %g, EC50 %.2g", sets$Emax, sets$EC50) sets$S0 <- sprintf("Emax/EC50 = %g", sets$Emax / sets$EC50) cc <- 10^seq(-0.5, 3, by = 0.25) climb <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(sets)), function(k) data.frame(sets[k, ], cmax = cc, t = sapply(cc * V, t_climb, Emax = sets$Emax[k], EC50 = sets$EC50[k])))) climb$set <- factor(climb$set, levels = sets$set) lines_C <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(sets$Emax / sets$EC50), function(s0) data.frame(S0 = sprintf("Emax/EC50 = %g", s0), cmax = cc, t = log(f_loq * s0 * cc / (1 - f_loq)) / ke))) %>% filter(t > 0) pC <- ggplot(climb, aes(cmax, t, colour = S0)) + geom_line(data = lines_C, linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(shape = set), size = 2.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal3[1:2], name = NULL) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 2, 15), name = NULL) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Cmax, mg/L, log scale", y = "Day the count climbs above 5%", title = "C. Dose escalation") + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.text = element_text(size = 8)) (pA | pC) / pB + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A: the model. Fall | first one to two days | $t_{1/2,\rm fall} \approx \dfrac{\ln 2}{k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})}$ | $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$ | | 3. Floor | while $C \gg EC_{50}$ | $B \approx \dfrac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}}$ | $E_{\max}$ | | 4. Climb back | when $E(C)$ falls to $(1-f)/f$ | $t_f \approx \dfrac{1}{k_e} \ln \dfrac{f\, S_0\, C_{\max}}{1 - f}$ | $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$ | | 5. Tail | once $S_0 C \ll 1$ | $B_0 - B \propto e^{-k_{\rm out} t}$ | $k_{\rm out}$ | | Low dose | $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ throughout | nadir depth $\approx S_0 C_{\max} (k_{\rm out}/k_e)^{k_e/(k_e - k_{\rm out})}$ | $S_0$, $k_{\rm out}$ | : The five parts of the curve, with $f$ the fraction of baseline at which the count is read, here the 5% quantification limit {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,38,22]"} ### 2.1 Two rates decide the shape Dividing the model equation of Section 1 by $B$ gives $$ \frac{d \ln B}{dt} = k_{\rm out} \left( \frac{B_0}{B} - 1 - E(C) \right) $$ At any fixed concentration this pulls $B$ toward its quasi-steady state $B_{\rm qss} = B_0 / (1 + E(C))$, the level at which the bracket is zero, at the rate $k_{\rm out}(1 + E(C))$. The concentration itself falls at the rate $k_e = CL/V$. Which of the two rates is larger decides whether $B$ keeps up with the drug: - **$k_{\rm out}(1 + E) \gg k_e$**: $B$ follows $B_{\rm qss}$, and its level at any time is fixed by the concentration at that time. - **$k_{\rm out}(1 + E) \ll k_e$**: $B$ lags the drug, and its return is limited by its own turnover. The first rate changes by a factor of $1 + E_{\max}$ over the course of one dose. With the values of Section 1 it is $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max}) = 3.0$ per day at the start, 45 times $k_e = 0.067$ per day, and $k_{\rm out} = 0.02$ per day at the end, 0.3 times $k_e$. The curve begins fast and ends slow, and that ordering is why its parts separate. Peletier, Gabrielsson and Haag (references, entry 15) put the same point in dimensionless form: with time scaled by $1/k_e$ and the count by $B_0$, the whole curve is fixed by three numbers, $\kappa = k_{\rm out}/k_e$, $E_{\max}$, and $C_{\max}/EC_{50}$. The two rates above are $\kappa$ and $\kappa(1 + E_{\max})$ in those units. Krzyzanski and Jusko (entry 17) show the same competition for an infusion: the response approaches its steady state at the slower of $k_e$ and $k_{\rm out}(1 + E)$. Sections 2.3 to 2.8 note where each result below is already in these papers. Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997 (entry 13), the bolus paper the others build on, has not been read. The model also depends on concentration only through $C/EC_{50}$, so scaling the dose and $EC_{50}$ by the same factor leaves the curve unchanged. Sharma and Jusko made the same observation for all four indirect-response models in 1996 (references, entry 12). ### 2.2 The baseline $B(0) = B_0$, and $B \to B_0$ as the drug clears. The baseline carries $B_0$ and nothing else. ### 2.3 The fall For the first days, $t \ll 1/k_e = 15$ days, the concentration has barely moved from $C_{\max}$, so the coefficient in the model equation is constant and the equation is linear: $$ B(t) = B_{\rm ss} + (B_0 - B_{\rm ss})\, e^{-k_f t}, \qquad k_f = k_{\rm out}\big(1 + E(C_{\max})\big), \qquad B_{\rm ss} = \frac{B_0}{1 + E(C_{\max})} $$ The initial slope of $\ln B$ is $-k_{\rm out} E(C_{\max})$, and the time to fall to half of baseline is $$ t_{1/2,\rm fall} = \frac{1}{k_f} \ln \frac{B_0 - B_{\rm ss}}{B_0/2 - B_{\rm ss}} \approx \frac{\ln 2}{k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})} \quad \text{for } C_{\max} \gg EC_{50},\ E_{\max} \gg 1 $$ **The fall carries the product $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$.** $EC_{50}$ enters it only through $E(C_{\max}) = E_{\max}/(1 + EC_{50}/C_{\max})$, a 1% correction at $C_{\max} = 100 \times EC_{50}$. With the values here, $t_{1/2,\rm fall}$ is 0.23 days, five and a half hours, and the fall is 99% complete by day 1.5. Both pieces are published. Sharma and Jusko 1996 (entry 12, their Eq. 26) give the large-dose initial slope as $-k_{\rm out} B_0 S_{\max}$, the slope above in absolute units. Peletier et al. (entry 15, their Eq. 32) prove that for every dose $$ B(t) > \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}} \left(1 + E_{\max}\, e^{-k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max}) t}\right) $$ and that the curve converges to this bound as the dose grows. The bound is the fall formula above with $E(C_{\max})$ replaced by $E_{\max}$. ### 2.4 The floor After the fall, $k_f \gg k_e$ and $B$ tracks the quasi-steady state: $$ B(t) \approx \frac{B_0}{1 + E\big(C(t)\big)} \approx \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}} \quad \text{while } C(t) \gg EC_{50} $$ **The floor carries $E_{\max}$**, given $B_0$, and is the large-dose limit of the nadir in Sharma and Jusko 1996 (entry 12, their Eq. 14). With $E_{\max} = 150$ it is 1.3 cells/µL. A floor is quantifiable only if it sits above the limit $f B_0$, which needs $E_{\max} < 1/f - 1$: below 19 for a limit at 5% of baseline, below 39 for one at 2.5%. ### 2.5 The climb back The count stays on the quasi-steady state as the drug clears, and crosses the fraction $f$ of baseline when $E(C) = (1 - f)/f$. Solving the $E_{\max}$ function for that concentration, $$ C_f = EC_{50}\, \frac{1 - f}{f E_{\max} - (1 - f)} $$ and with $C(t) = C_{\max} e^{-k_e t}$ the crossing time is $$ t_f = \frac{1}{k_e} \ln \frac{C_{\max}}{C_f} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{k_e} \ln \frac{f\, S_0\, C_{\max}}{1 - f}}_{\text{depends on } S_0 \text{ only}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{k_e} \ln\left(1 - \frac{1 - f}{f E_{\max}}\right)}_{\text{the only place } E_{\max} \text{ enters alone}} $$ **The climb back carries $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$**, given $k_e$ from the PK. The second term is the only information about $E_{\max}$ separately that survives in the recovery. With $f = 0.05$ it is $-2.0$ days at $E_{\max} = 150$, $-7.2$ days at 50 and $-0.6$ days at 450: a shift of a few days in a crossing that happens around day 100, read through 30% residual error from monthly samples. This term is why the designs of Section 6 with a first sample at day 7 leave $E_{\max}$ at 90% to over 800% relative standard error rather than at infinity. Two conditions hold the formula together. The count must still be on the quasi-steady state at the crossing, which needs $k_{\rm out}/f \gg k_e$, or $f \ll k_{\rm out}/k_e = 0.3$; when it fails the count lags and the crossing comes a few days later than the formula says. And the crossing concentration must be below $EC_{50}$, which holds whenever $f E_{\max} \gg 1$. Across a dose escalation, $\partial t_f / \partial \ln C_{\max} = 1/k_e$, so each ten-fold step in dose delays the climb by $\ln 10 / k_e = 34.5$ days, 3.3 PK half-lives, whatever $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are. This is Levy's dose-duration relation from 1966 (references, entry 11): the duration of an effect is linear in log dose, the slope gives the elimination rate, and the line extrapolates to zero duration at a threshold dose, here $C_{\max} = (1 - f)/(f S_0)$. Levy derived it for a direct effect with a threshold. The indirect-response model gives the same line because the count follows the quasi-steady state, which is a direct function of concentration. Panel C of the figure shows the line and the points falling on it, with the lowest doses bending away where the count never reaches the quasi-steady state. Peletier et al. (entry 15, their Eqs. 42 to 44) prove the general form of this. As the dose grows, the recovery part of the curve converges to a fixed shape that translates in time by $\ln(C_{\max}/EC_{50})/k_e$, a travelling wave. The crossing time $t_f$ is where that shape crosses $f$, worked out under the quasi-steady state; the shape itself depends on $E_{\max}$ and $\kappa$, which is where the correction term above comes from. ### 2.6 The tail Once $S_0 C \ll 1$, the drug effect is negligible and the model is $dB/dt = k_{\rm out}(B_0 - B)$, so $$ B_0 - B(t) \propto e^{-k_{\rm out} t} $$ **The tail carries $k_{\rm out}$.** This needs $k_{\rm out} < k_e$. If the cells turned over faster than the drug cleared, the count would follow the drug down to baseline and the tail would carry $k_e$ instead, the indirect-response version of flip-flop kinetics. Here $k_{\rm out}/k_e = 0.3$. ### 2.7 Doses that stay below EC50 When $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ the drug effect is in its linear range for the whole curve, $$ E(C) = \frac{S_0 C}{1 + C/EC_{50}} = S_0 C \left(1 - \frac{C}{EC_{50}} + \dots\right) \approx S_0 C $$ and the model becomes $dB/dt = k_{\rm out} B_0 - k_{\rm out}(1 + S_0 C) B$, which contains $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ only as their ratio. **The whole curve of a low dose, nadir included, carries $S_0$ and $k_{\rm out}$**, with a correction of relative size $C_{\max}/EC_{50}$. When the depletion is also shallow, $S_0 C_{\max} \ll 1$, the depth $\varepsilon = 1 - B/B_0$ obeys $d\varepsilon/dt \approx k_{\rm out}(S_0 C - \varepsilon)$, which has the same solution as an oral one-compartment PK model: $$ \varepsilon(t) = \frac{k_{\rm out}\, S_0 C_{\max}}{k_e - k_{\rm out}} \left(e^{-k_{\rm out} t} - e^{-k_e t}\right), \qquad \varepsilon_{\max} = S_0 C_{\max} \left(\frac{k_{\rm out}}{k_e}\right)^{k_e/(k_e - k_{\rm out})} $$ at $t = \ln(k_e/k_{\rm out})/(k_e - k_{\rm out})$, day 26 here. The nadir depth is proportional to $S_0 C_{\max}$, with a factor of 0.18 set by the two rates. The same solution and nadir time are Eqs. 34 and 35 of Peletier et al. (entry 15), for the linear drug effect. ### 2.8 The area between baseline and curve The area between the baseline and the B-cell curve, $\int_0^\infty (B_0 - B)\,dt$, is the summary Sharma and Jusko (entry 12, their Eq. 22) and Peletier et al. (entry 15, their Eq. 49) give for large doses: $$ \text{area} \sim \frac{B_0}{k_e} \frac{E_{\max}}{1 + E_{\max}} \ln\left(1 + \frac{C_{\max}}{EC_{50}}\right) \quad \text{as } C_{\max} \to \infty $$ Peletier et al. note that $E_{\max}$ can be read from the slope of the area against log dose. **For a B-cell depleting agent the slope carries almost no $E_{\max}$:** the factor $E_{\max}/(1 + E_{\max})$ is 0.98 at $E_{\max} = 50$ and 0.993 at 150. The formula is also a leading-order statement, and at practical doses the omitted constant is larger than the term kept. The table compares it with the area measured on the ODE solution for the three parameter sets of panel C that share $S_0 = 150$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} area_ode <- function(dose, Emax, EC50) { tt <- seq(0, 3000, by = 0.5); sum(B0 - sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)) * 0.5 } area <- expand.grid(k = 1:3, cmax = c(1, 10, 100, 1000)) %>% mutate(Emax = sets$Emax[k], EC50 = sets$EC50[k], ode = mapply(function(c, e, ec) area_ode(c * V, e, ec), cmax, Emax, EC50), formula = B0 / ke * Emax / (1 + Emax) * log(1 + cmax / EC50)) %>% select(cmax, Emax, EC50, ode, formula) knitr::kable(area, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0, 0), col.names = c("Cmax, mg/L", "Emax", "EC50, mg/L", "Area on the ODE, cells·day/µL", "Large-dose formula"), caption = "Area between baseline and B-cell curve, from the ODE solution and from the large-dose formula, for three parameter sets with Emax/EC50 = 150") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Area between baseline and B-cell curve, from the ODE solution and from the large-dose formula, for three parameter sets with Emax/EC50 = 150 | Cmax, mg/L| Emax| EC50, mg/L| Area on the ODE, cells·day/µL| Large-dose formula| |----------:|----:|----------:|-----------------------------:|------------------:| | 1| 50| 0.33| 21407| 4077| | 1| 150| 1.00| 21715| 2066| | 1| 450| 3.00| 21818| 861| | 10| 50| 0.33| 28222| 10100| | 10| 150| 1.00| 28615| 7146| | 10| 450| 3.00| 28738| 4389| | 100| 50| 0.33| 34999| 16786| | 100| 150| 1.00| 35481| 13754| | 100| 450| 3.00| 35631| 10585| | 1000| 50| 0.33| 41771| 23549| | 1000| 150| 1.00| 42343| 20589| | 1000| 450| 3.00| 42523| 17398| ::: ::: The measured area moves by $B_0 \ln 10 / k_e$ per ten-fold dose, as the formula's slope says, and at a given dose it is nearly the same for all three sets: like the climb back, it follows $S_0$. The formula's level is low by a factor that shrinks only logarithmically with dose. The omitted constant is of order $(B_0/k_e)\ln E_{\max} + B_0/k_{\rm out}$, the extra time for the drug to fall from $EC_{50}$ to $EC_{50}/E_{\max}$ plus the lag of the recovery, and with $E_{\max} = 150$ and slow turnover both are large. The area is computed over the whole curve, including the part below the limit, so it is not an observable a B-cell study can use directly in any case. ### 2.9 Checking the formulas against the ODE solution Each formula above is an approximation, and each can be checked by solving the model and measuring the feature it predicts. The tail and low-dose formulas are close to exact. ### 2.10 What is identifiable and what is not **Structurally, the model is identifiable**: with noise-free observations at every time, the floor gives $E_{\max}$ and the fall gives it again, and $EC_{50} = E_{\max}/S_0$ follows. Janzén et al. (references, entry 16) checked a family of turnover and receptor-binding models formally and found the same, with the same failure in practice: when the effect saturates, the two parameters of the saturating function are estimated with high uncertainty and correlation, and the ratio is estimated well. **The loss of identifiability here is practical**, made by the quantification limit and the sampling schedule, and the parts of Section 2.2 to 2.7 say exactly which samples remove which parameter. The identification chain itself is in Sharma and Jusko 1998 (entry 4, their Table 1), as a graphical recipe: read the baseline, the initial slope and the large-dose nadir; the nadir gives $S_{\max}$, the slope with $S_{\max}$ gives $k_{\rm in}$ and so $k_{\rm out}$, and the concentration at the time of the nadir gives $SC_{50}$. The design they say it needs is two or more bolus doses, one high enough for full stimulation, and the baseline. For B cells the first two readings are the ones a study loses: the nadir sits below the limit, and the initial slope is over before a weekly sample. | Part of the curve | Carries | Observed when | Usual B-cell study | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | Baseline | $B_0$ | always | ✅ | | Fall | $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$ | samples in the first one to two days, above the limit | ❌ first sample at a week | | Floor | $E_{\max}$ | $E_{\max} < 1/f - 1$ | ❌ below the limit | | Climb back | $S_0$; $E_{\max}$ only through a few-day correction | samples through recovery; $k_e$ from PK | ✅ | | Tail | $k_{\rm out}$ | samples until repopulation | ✅ | | Low-dose cohort | $S_0$, $k_{\rm out}$ | any dose with $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ | ✅ when present, and adds no $E_{\max}$ | : Which parameter each part of the curve identifies, and whether a typical study sees it - ✅ **Identified by any design that follows the recovery to the end:** $B_0$, $k_{\rm out}$, and $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. - ⚠️ **$E_{\max}$: only from samples during the fall, or from a floor above the limit.** Without either, it is left with the climb-back correction of Section 2.5, a few days on a hundred-day timing. - ❌ **$EC_{50}$ on its own: from no part of the curve.** It is identified exactly when $E_{\max}$ is, as $E_{\max}/S_0$, and with the same precision or worse. The arithmetic of a large Emax At a steady concentration $C$, the count settles at $$ \frac{B_{ss}}{B_0} = \frac{1}{1 + E(C)} = \frac{1}{1 + E_{\max} C/(EC_{50} + C)} $$ so that half-maximal depletion, $B_{ss} = B_0/2$, needs $E = 1$, which is at $$ C_{1/2} = \frac{EC_{50}}{E_{\max} - 1} $$ For $E_{\max} = 150$ that is $EC_{50}/149$. The concentration that halves the drug's *effect on the rate* and the concentration that halves the *cell count* are two orders of magnitude apart. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cc <- 10^seq(-4, 2, length.out = 300) dep <- bind_rows(lapply(c(1, 10, 150), function(em) data.frame(Emax = em, C = cc, frac = 1 / (1 + em * cc / (1 + cc))))) dep$Emax <- factor(paste("Emax =", dep$Emax), levels = paste("Emax =", c(1, 10, 150))) ggplot(dep, aes(C, 100 * frac, colour = Emax)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") + geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) + scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-4:2), labels = c("0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100")) + annotate("text", x = 1, y = 95, label = "EC50", hjust = -0.1, size = 3, colour = "grey40") + annotate("text", x = 1e-4, y = 5, label = "5% LOQ", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = "grey40") + labs(x = "Concentration, multiples of EC50, log scale", y = "Steady-state B cells, % of baseline") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Steady-state depletion against concentration for three values of Emax. The vertical line is EC50. Below $C_{1/2}/10$ the effect is small and linear in $C$ with slope $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. Above $EC_{50}$ the count is below the limit whatever $C$ is. In between, the count is quantifiable and its level depends on $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ separately. That band, roughly $EC_{50}/1500$ to $EC_{50}/15$ here, is where a cohort would have to sit for the nadir to identify the two parameters, and no therapeutic dose sits there. Krzyzanski and Jusko made the same point for infusions in 1998 (references, entry 17): two steady states give $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ only if their concentrations are not both well above $EC_{50}$. ## 5. Where the information lives The sensitivity of the log count to each log parameter, along the top-dose profile, says what each observation can tell the estimator. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tt <- seq(0, 336, by = 1); h <- 1e-4 f0 <- sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt) sens <- data.frame(day = tt, Emax = (log(sim_B(300, Emax * exp(h), EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h, EC50 = (log(sim_B(300, Emax, EC50 * exp(h), kout, B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h, kout = (log(sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout * exp(h), B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h, B = f0) blq <- range(sens$day[sens$B < 0.05 * B0]) sl <- pivot_longer(sens, c(Emax, EC50, kout), names_to = "parameter", values_to = "s") sl$parameter <- factor(sl$parameter, levels = c("Emax", "EC50", "kout")) ggplot(sl, aes(day, s, colour = parameter)) + annotate("rect", xmin = blq[1], xmax = blq[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "grey30") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) + labs(x = "Day", y = "d log B / d log parameter") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sensitivity of log B-cell count to log Emax, log EC50 and log k_out over time after a dose with Cmax = 100 × EC50. Shaded region: count below a 5%-of-baseline limit, where no observation exists.](ec50-identifiability_files/figure-html/sens-1.png){width=624} ::: ::: Three regions, and each one identifies one thing. **Days 0 to 3, the fall.** Sensitivity to $E_{\max}$ and to $k_{\rm out}$ are both large and equal, and sensitivity to $EC_{50}$ is near zero. At high concentration the loss rate is $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$, so the speed of the fall identifies the product $k_{\rm out} E_{\max}$ and nothing about $EC_{50}$. This is the only place $E_{\max}$ appears without $EC_{50}$ beside it. **Days 4 to 80, the floor.** Everything is below the limit. No observations, no information. **Days 80 to 200, the recovery.** Sensitivity to $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are equal and opposite: raising one or lowering the other shifts the curve the same way. Recovery begins when $E(C)$ falls to order 1, which happens at $C \approx EC_{50}/E_{\max}$, so this region identifies the ratio and only the ratio. The likelihood ridge The Fisher information is a local statement. The shape of the objective function over $(E_{\max}, EC_{50})$ with $k_{\rm out}$ and $B_0$ held at truth shows the same thing globally. Ofatumumab is the case with cohorts in the band: the 3 mg and 10 mg subcutaneous arms gave partial and delayed depletion, subcutaneous absorption slows the fall so that weekly samples see it, and 1,486 patients did the rest. Rituximab at full dose is the ridge, with a 13-fold interval on $ED_{50}$ and an upper bound on $E_{\max}$ four times the estimate. Inebilizumab is the ridge recognized and dealt with: the estimator put $EC_{50}$ below the PK assay, which is where Section 4 says the band is, and the authors fit the slope instead. Two of the five took the route around the problem: fix the binding constant from in vitro measurements and let the model's potency come from the literature rather than the data. That is a legitimate answer to "what is $EC_{50}$", and it is not an estimate. ## 9. The slope parameterization Schoemaker, van Gerven and Cohen showed in 1998 that when the data do not approach $E_{\max}$, the parameter $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, the initial slope of the $E_{\max}$ curve, is estimable with good precision while its two factors are not, and proposed reporting it (references, entry 1). The inebilizumab model's $k = \text{slope} \cdot \log C$ is the same idea in a form that stays finite at high concentration. For everything downstream of the B-cell count, the slope is enough. The duration of depletion, the time to repopulate to a fraction of baseline, depends on when $E(C)$ falls to order 1, which is at $C \approx 1/S_0$, and on $k_{\rm out}$. Fitting the slope model and the $E_{\max}$ model to the same sparse data and predicting the duration across the studied dose range: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trep <- function(dose, form = "emax", S = 0, Cref = 1) { tt <- seq(0, 500, by = 1) B <- sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt, form = form, S = S, Cref = Cref) i <- which.min(B); j <- which(B[i:length(B)] >= 0.2 * B0)[1]; if (is.na(j)) NA else tt[i + j - 1] } Cref <- 0.1 S_match <- Emax / EC50 * Cref # equal initial slope: S/Cref = Emax/EC50 dd <- 10^seq(-1.5, 2.5, length.out = 17) tr <- bind_rows( data.frame(model = "Emax, EC50 (true)", dose = dd, trep = sapply(dd, trep)), data.frame(model = "Log-linear slope", dose = dd, trep = sapply(dd, trep, form = "slope", S = S_match, Cref = Cref))) ggplot(tr, aes(dose, trep, colour = model)) + annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 300, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "grey30") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.8) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal3[1:2], name = NULL) + scale_x_log10() + annotate("text", x = 30, y = 20, label = "studied dose range", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + labs(x = "Dose, mg, log scale", y = "Days to repopulate to 20% of baseline") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time to repopulate to 20% of baseline against dose, from the true Emax model and from a log-linear slope model with its slope matched to the true initial slope. What a study needs if it wants EC50 Stated as requirements, in the order they would be dropped from a protocol. 1. **B-cell samples on days 1 and 3 after the first dose.** The speed of the fall is the only observation that separates $E_{\max}$ from $EC_{50}$ at a therapeutic dose. With antibody-dependent lysis the fall is hours to days, and a first sample at a week arrives after it. 2. **B cells monthly until repopulation is complete in most patients.** The tail identifies $k_{\rm out}$, and without $k_{\rm out}$ the fall identifies nothing. 3. **A PK assay whose limit is below $EC_{50}/E_{\max}$**, or a willingness to extrapolate the PK tail by a factor of a hundred and say so. Recovery starts at concentrations the assay may never see. 4. **A cohort at a dose whose nadir is quantifiable and whose concentration sits inside the band of Section 4**, if the design can afford one. This is what ofatumumab had. A cohort below the band informs the slope and not the factors; a cohort above it is censored. 5. **Failing 1 and 4, fit the slope.** Report $S_0$ with its interval, state that $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are identified as a ratio, and let anyone who needs the factors fix one of them from in vitro binding. ## 11. What this means for the ITP project Section 6.2 of the [ITP-PK-Platelet specification](../imm-itp-pk-platelet/specification.qmd) fits a B-cell layer to a dose escalation of three to six patients per level, first sample at a week, in order to carry the duration of depletion forward to a platelet model. Sections 5 and 6 here say that design identifies the slope and $k_{\rm out}$ at a usable precision and identifies neither $E_{\max}$ nor $EC_{50}$; that Section 8 of the specification is right to parameterize by the slope; and that if the escalation protocol can add days 1 and 3, the $E_{\max}$ form becomes fittable at about 10% RSE across five cohorts, at the cost of two blood draws. ## 12. Open questions - **Sigmoidicity.** A Hill coefficient above 1 sharpens the band of Section 4 and makes the recovery start more abruptly. Whether it is identifiable alongside the slope at these designs has not been checked. - **Subcutaneous dosing.** Absorption over days slows the fall and moves the information of Section 5's first region into the first week, which is presumably part of why ofatumumab's model could see it. The simulations here are intravenous. - **Censoring handled properly.** Dropping observations below the limit throws away the statement that they are below it. A likelihood with censored terms would recover some information at the floor, and the comparison between designs is not expected to change. - **Between-patient variability.** The Fisher information here is for a population with fixed parameters. With 50 to 126% CV on the recovery rate in published models, the precision numbers in Section 6 are optimistic by a factor that a population-design tool would give.
